A sequencer remembers a line of notes and plays it back. The machines on this page all do that, but each one asks you to
write the line in a different way: turning eight knobs, pressing a key for each pitch and then tapping in the rhythm,
typing numbers, or lighting up sixteen buttons. How you enter a line changes which lines are easy to write. In practice it
changes what music people made with each machine.

Each machine is rebuilt here in the browser. The panels are drawn after the real ones and are not copies; the names belong
to their makers. You can write a line on one machine and turn it into the nearest line on another. A report then tells
you, for every part of the line, whether it is **the same**, **close** or **lost**, and why, with the manual page.
Anything the manuals do not say is this page's own choice and is marked so.

## The five sequencers

<div class="sqc"></div>

**How to use it.** Pick an **Example**, or choose the machines under **From** and **To**. Press **▶** to hear either machine,
or one after the other. Edit the top panel and the bottom one follows. **⇅ Swap** makes the bottom machine the starting
point. Point at a line of the report to light up the controls it is about on both panels. Coloured outlines show
<span class="sqc-key" style="background:#2e9e6a">the same</span>, <span class="sqc-key" style="background:#d4a72c;color:#222">close</span> and
<span class="sqc-key" style="background:#c8443a">lost</span>. Every machine plays the same simple voice (a saw or square wave
into a low-pass filter). That way you hear the *sequence*, not five different synthesizers.

## How each one is programmed

- **The 960-style step sequencer** (after the Moog 960). There are 8 stages in 3 rows of knobs. Each knob sets a voltage,
  and the oscillator moves the sequencer on one stage per cycle (Q960 data sheet pp. 1, 3). Row A here sets pitch at 1 volt
  an octave. Row B goes to the filter. Row C can be switched to the clock: each volt doubles the speed, so a stage with a
  higher row-C knob is shorter (p. 4). Each stage can be **Normal**, **Skip** or **Stop** (p. 3). Every stage starts the
  envelope with the oscillator's pulse, which is on for 90 % of the cycle (pp. 3, 5). So there are no rests, and every note
  has the same gate length.
- **TB-303 pattern write.** You write the pitches first: in **PITCH MODE** you press the keys in order, with transpose
  **DOWN** / **UP** for other octaves. Then you write the rhythm in **TIME MODE**, sixteen presses of note, tie or rest,
  and no sound plays while you do it (TB-303 manual pp. 5, 14-15; the TB-03 manual names the three keys). Accent and slide
  go on a note while you tap back through the pitches (pp. 40-43). The pitches are used in order by the *note* steps. Add
  a rest and every pitch after it moves one note later. Try it on the panel.
- **MC-202.** Two channels. Each note has a pitch, a **step time** (how long until the next note) and a **gate time** (how
  long it sounds), counted 24 to a quarter note (MC-202 manual pp. 10, 15-16). Accent and portamento are stored with the
  notes. Portamento is entered on the *second* of the two notes it joins (p. 29). On the 303, slide is marked on the
  first.
- **MC-4 MicroComposer.** You type numbers on a calculator keypad, one whole memory at a time: all the pitches (CV-1), then
  all the step times, then all the gate times (MC-4 manual pp. 13-18). Pitches are numbers counting up the keyboard (p. 9).
  The time base is 120 to a beat, so a 16th note is 30 (p. 10). There are four channels, each with CV-1, CV-2 and a gate.
  CV-2 can drive "the VCF, the VCA, or any other" module (p. 11).
- **Elektron-style trig sequencer** (after the Digitakt II). Sixteen trig keys a page. A **note trig** plays a note and a
  **lock trig** only changes settings (Digitakt II manual p. 41). Hold a trig and turn a knob to **parameter-lock** that
  setting on that step alone (p. 47). **Trig conditions** decide each time round whether a trig plays: `1:2` plays on the
  first of every two loops, `1ST` only the first time, `PRE` if the last condition was true, and so on (p. 48). **Micro
  timing** nudges a trig off its step (p. 45).

## What carries over

| From → To | Usually the same | Usually close | Usually lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| TB-303 → 960 | pitches | accents (as row-B filter voltage) | slides, rests, steps 9-16 |
| 960 → TB-303 | even 16th rhythm, pitches set to a semitone | knobs between two semitones (rounded) | row-B filter values |
| MC-202 → TB-303 | pitches, accents, slides | gate lengths (become whole steps) | channel 2 |
| MC-4 → TB-303 | pitches on the 16th grid | triplets and swing (moved onto a grid) | CV-2, channels 2-4 |
| MC-4 → MC-202 | step / gate idea, two channels | times rounded from 1/120 to 1/24 of a beat | channels 3-4, CV-2 |
| Elektron → anything else | the loop you chose | micro timing, velocity | trig conditions, probability, parameter locks |

The worked examples show each row. Change a few things and watch the report change.

## Reading the pictures

- **Piano roll**: what each machine actually plays, the *From* machine in outline and the *To* machine filled. A dashed or
  coloured line between two notes is a slide or portamento. Thick bars are accents.
- **Timing grid**: one beat, with a tick wherever each machine can start a note. The 303 has 4 (or the TB-03's triplet
  grid), the MC-202 24, the MC-4 120 and the Elektron 4 plus micro-timing marks. The 960 has a shaded bar, because its
  stage lengths come from turning knobs and are not counted. The dots are where this line's notes fall.
- **Lanes**: for every note, its velocity, accent, slide, gate length as a share of the step, and the filter value (yellow
  dots are lock trigs).

## Analog step sequencers

The Wikipedia article "Music sequencer", citing Pinch and Trocco, says analog sequencers were used for "repeated
minimalistic phrases" in the music of Tangerine Dream and Giorgio Moroder, and later in trance. The Moog 960 here is
rebuilt from the data sheet of the Synthesizers.com Q960, a module that its maker calls "functionally equivalent to the
Moog 960" (p. 5). No Moog 960 manual was found.

## MC-8 and MC-4: typing music in numbers

According to Wikipedia ("Roland MC-8 Microcomposer"), Roland's MC-8 (1977) was the first microprocessor-based digital
sequencer, and Yellow Magic Orchestra, from 1978, are its earliest known users. The MC-4 (1981, US$3,295) followed it
("Roland MC-4 Microcomposer"). It used numeric entry with middle C as 24, a time base of 120 to a quarter (a 16th is 30)
and four channels. Its memory was lost at power-off and saved to cassette or the MTR-100. Users named there include Vince
Clarke on Yazoo's *Upstairs at Eric's* (1982) and Erasure's *Chorus* (1991). Clarke called it "a pig to program but well
worth it". Also named are YMO, Kraftwerk, Tomita, the Human League and Depeche Mode.

## TB-303: the bass line that failed, then became acid

From Wikipedia ("Roland TB-303"): Roland released it in 1981. It was designed by Tadao Kikumoto, cost US$395, and was
marketed to replace a bass guitar. It was a commercial failure and was discontinued in 1984. A saw or square wave goes into
a 24 dB-per-octave low-pass filter, and it stores 64 patterns and 7 songs. It became the sound of **acid house**, and is
also tied to **Chicago house** and **techno**. Records named in the article:

- Charanjit Singh, *Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat* (1982)
- Bappi Lahiri's film songs of 1983: "Koi Lutera", "Aah Ha Oonh Hun", "Tum Tum Tumba"
- Orange Juice, "Rip It Up" (1983); Ryo Kawasaki, *Lucky Lady* (1983)
- Phuture, "Acid Tracks" (1987)
- Hardfloor, "Acperience" (1992); Josh Wink, "Higher State of Consciousness" (1995)
- Daft Punk, "Da Funk"; Fatboy Slim, "Everybody Needs a 303" (1996)

## MC-202: the first groovebox

From Wikipedia ("Roland MC-202"): Roland made it from 1983 to 1985 and it cost $595. It is called the first groovebox: a
two-track sequencer with a built-in synth. Each note has pitch, length, gate, accent and slide. It saved to tape through a
tape interface, and its successor was the MC-303 (1996).

## Elektron-style sequencing

This page says nothing about the history of Elektron's machines. Only their manual has been read, not a history source.
What it rebuilds is the Digitakt II's way of entering a line: note and lock trigs, parameter locks, trig conditions,
micro timing, length and speed. Speed 3/4X is how the manual suggests playing triplets, and 2X gives 32nd notes (p. 46).

## Rebuild a line from a video

Under the widget is a list of YouTube videos in which someone rebuilds a known song's sequence on one of these machines
or a close relative. Each was checked to exist. Nobody has checked whether each video's line matches the record. No
video of a Moog 960 itself was found, so the analog list uses other step sequencers.

1. Press **Use** beside a video. It chooses that machine and fills in the song, artist and link.
2. Rebuild the line by ear on the top panel. Write the time in the video where the line is heard in **At**.
3. Press **⤓ Export**. The file is a small JSON record (`kind: "sequence"`, `version: 1`, the machine, its settings, the
   song, the artist and the source). Hand it in, or **⤒ Import** it later to carry on.
4. Turn it into another machine and write down what was lost.

## What is checked and what is not

Checked against the manuals, with pages in the report: how each machine enters notes, the stage, step and grid sizes, step
and gate times, the MC-4's time base and channels, the 303's pitch and time memories, accent and slide or portamento,
trig types, parameter locks, trig conditions, micro timing, speed and swing range. The Roland manuals are scans, cited by
the PDF's page number.

This page's own choices, not from the manuals: the 303's key range here (C2 to C5), the MC-202 gate keys' lengths (the
table did not scan cleanly), the MC-4's CV-2 scale (0-100), treating gate 0 as a rest on the MC-4, micro timing in 1/24 of
a step (the Digitakt manual does not give the size), how swing moves the off-beat 16ths, slide time, and the shared voice.
The voice is not a model of any of these machines. Nobody has yet compared the playback with the real instruments.
